To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
optic ataxia is a disorder that affects the representation of space around the body, and that this representation is modulated by the location of the body part and of the target in the visual field.

optic ataxia is characterized by an impaired representation of reachable space in the visual peripersonal field and that this representation is especially affected in the lower part of the visual field.

optic ataxia affects both the perception of the hand and the perception of the target in the lower visual fields, and that this effect is enhanced in conditions where the target and the hands are both perceived in the visual field periphery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
optic ataxia as an impairment of the representation of the peripersonal environment.
the relationship between hand-to-target distances and the representation of perispace, and it highlights the importance of peripheral vision in the processing of reachable distances.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the difficulties of optic ataxic patients to perceive hand-target distance and to perceive reachable space are due to their inability to integrate visual information about the hand and the visual space, especially when the hand is not fixated and/or when it is in the lower visual space.
optic ataxia is a disorder of spatial perception, and the deficit in reaching movements is a secondary consequence.

optic ataxia, as a disorder of spatial perception, affects the perception of reachable space, and that the impairment of the representation of perispace depends on the spatial position of the target and the body parts involved in the task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
optic ataxia affects not only reaching, but also the perception of reachable space, especially in a condition in which the hand is perceived in peripheral vision and in the lower visual hemifield.

the optic ataxia deficit is not a general problem in perceiving target location in space but a specific difficulty in perceiving target-to-hand distances, which is enhanced when both the target (or the hand) is perceived in the visual lower periphery.
patients with optic ataxia are impaired in processing the hand-to-target distances when both the hand and the targets are in the lower visual periphery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the representation of pericentric space, which is a fundamental part of the visuomotor system, is not spared in patients with optic ataxia.
optic ataxia can be seen as a deficit in the representation of the space around the hand.
optic ataxia is not a unitary syndrome.
